data.title: Acquired melanocytic nevus (mole) — viva
data.summary: Nevi & hamartomas · 9 viva questions with answers
data.body:
_Viva questions for the case: **Acquired melanocytic nevus (mole)** (Nevi & hamartomas)_

**Q1. What is an acquired melanocytic naevus?**
- Benign proliferation of naevus cells (melanocytes) in nests, appearing after 6 months of age, increasing in childhood/young adulthood (peak in 3rd decade) and regressing in old age; number linked to sun exposure in childhood and genetics; fewer in dark skin

**Q2. Classify by histological level (life cycle).**
- Junctional: flat, uniformly brown, nests at dermo-epidermal junction (children)
- Compound: slightly raised brown papule, junctional + dermal nests
- Intradermal: dome-shaped skin-coloured/light-brown papule, often with hairs, dermal nests only with maturation (smaller, neurotised cells deeper) — adults, face
- Special types: blue naevus (dermal dendritic melanocytes — blue due to Tyndall effect), Spitz naevus, halo naevus, dysplastic (atypical/Clark's) naevus, recurrent naevus, acral naevus (parallel furrow pattern), Meyerson naevus (eczematous halo), combined naevus

**Q3. What is a dysplastic (atypical) naevus and the atypical mole syndrome?**
- Clinically atypical naevus: ≥5 mm, irregular/ill-defined border, variegated colour, flat component ('fried-egg'); histology — architectural disorder (bridging, lentiginous growth, shouldering), cytological atypia, lamellar fibroplasia
- Atypical mole syndrome / FAMMM (familial atypical multiple mole melanoma): >50–100 naevi, several atypical, family history of melanoma — CDKN2A (p16) mutations (also pancreatic cancer risk); lifelong surveillance with total body photography and dermoscopy

**Q4. Write a short note on Kamino bodies (PYQ).**
- Eosinophilic, PAS-positive, diastase-resistant, globular hyaline bodies (basement membrane material — collagen IV/laminin) at the dermo-epidermal junction above the nests in Spitz naevus; seen in ~60–80% — favour Spitz over melanoma when numerous and confluent

**Q5. What is a Spitz naevus?**
- Benign melanocytic naevus of spindle and/or epithelioid cells, children and young adults; dome-shaped pink-red or brown papule on face/legs growing quickly then stabilising; dermoscopy — starburst pattern (pigmented Reed naevus) or dotted vessels (pink)
- Histology: symmetric, well-circumscribed, maturation, Kamino bodies, clefts around junctional nests, epidermal hyperplasia
- Atypical Spitz tumours — uncertain potential; excision recommended in adults/atypical lesions

**Q6. Dermoscopy of benign naevi.**
- Reticular (network), globular, homogeneous (blue naevus), starburst (Spitz/Reed), parallel furrow (acral), peripheral rim of globules (growing naevus in children)
- Melanoma-specific structures: atypical network, negative network, irregular streaks, irregular dots/globules, blue-white veil, regression structures, atypical vessels, parallel ridge pattern (acral), shiny white lines

**Q7. What are the ABCDE warning signs?**
- Asymmetry, Border irregularity, Colour variegation, Diameter >6 mm, Evolution (change in size/shape/colour, symptoms) — plus 'ugly duckling' sign (lesion different from the patient's other naevi)
- Glasgow 7-point checklist: major — change in size, shape, colour; minor — diameter ≥7 mm, inflammation, oozing/bleeding, altered sensation

**Q8. Risk factors for melanoma related to naevi.**
- Number of common naevi (>100), atypical naevi (≥5), large congenital naevi, family history (CDKN2A, CDK4, BAP1, MITF), fair skin, sunburns, immunosuppression; in India, acral lentiginous melanoma is commonest (soles, nails — not UV-related)

**Q9. Management.**
- Benign naevi — reassurance; sun protection; monitor with photographs/dermoscopy
- Excision biopsy (narrow 2 mm margins, full thickness) for any suspicious lesion; do not shave/laser suspicious pigmented lesions
- Cosmetic removal: shave excision, punch, radiofrequency (only after confirming benign)
- Teach self-examination; total-body photography for many/atypical naevi

## Quick spotter facts
- Ugly duckling — biopsy
- Kamino bodies — Spitz naevus
- Acral lentiginous melanoma — commonest in India

_Sources: Previous-year PG question papers (Sahana P Raju, Solved Papers Dermatology); IADVL Textbook of Dermatology 5e (Melanocytic naevi; melanoma). Answers written in our own words; check with your teachers' preferences._
